lesson_title: How Many Edges Does a Tin Have?
hook_text: A tin can. How many faces, edges and corners? Most people get at least one of the three wrong.
clip_script: Pick up a tin can. Flat circle on top, flat circle on the bottom: 2 flat faces. The label wraps round 1 curved surface. Now the edges. An edge is where two surfaces meet, and on a tin the flat lid meets the curved side all the way round: that rim is an edge, and so is the bottom rim. 2 edges, curved ones. Corners? A corner is where edges meet, and the two rims never touch anything. 0 vertices. Two, one, two, zero. Now a ball. One curved surface, and that is it: no flat faces, no edges, no corners. That is why a ball rolls every way and a tin only rolls one way. Slice the tin across and you get a circle; slice it down the middle and you get a rectangle. Slice the ball anywhere and it is always a circle. Two, one, two, zero.
visual_style: A tin can rotates on a whiteboard as its flat faces, curved surface and two rims light up in turn; a ball glows with a single surface; a knife line slices each to reveal circles and a rectangle.
pacing: Count each part with a beat, a quick contrast with the ball, a crisp finish on the slices.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson for great circles, hemispheres, hollow pipes and the comparison with prisms and cones.
